title: 1 Clement
subtitle: the church of Rome writes to the church of Corinth about peace, order and the elders it threw out
lead: 1 Clement is a long letter that the church in Rome sent to the church in Corinth at the end of the first century, most probably in its last decade (Lake). Some members at Corinth had led a revolt and removed elders from their office, and Rome wrote to bring them back to peace. In Kirsopp Lake's words, it is "a letter sent by the church of Rome to the church of Corinth in consequence of trouble in the latter community which had led to the deposition of certain Presbyters." The letter never names its writer: it speaks as the church of God living as a resident alien in Rome (1:0). From the second century on, Christians said that Clement wrote it, a leader of the Roman church whom the early lists of bishops place third or fourth after the apostles.

The letter argues the way a sermon does, by example after example. Jealousy and envy, it says, killed Abel, drove Joseph into slavery and Moses into exile, and in Clement's own generation brought Peter and Paul to their deaths (3-6). It calls the Corinthians back to repentance, faith, hospitality and humility through Noah, Abraham, Lot, Rahab, the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 and David's Psalm 51 (7-18), and shows them a universe that keeps its order in harmony (20). It defends the resurrection with the seed and the phoenix (24-26), points to Jesus Christ the high priest (36), and holds up the ranks of an army, the parts of a body and the service of the Temple (37-41). Then it comes to the point: the apostles appointed overseers and deacons and arranged for other approved men to succeed them, so it is a sin to remove men who served without blame (42-44). It ends with a call to the ringleaders to step aside, a great prayer for the chosen, the suffering and the rulers (59-61), and the names of the messengers who carried it (65:1).

At the edge of the Bible. 1 Clement is not in the New Testament of the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Anglican, Reformed or Baptist churches, and this site translates it as an early Christian writing, never as Scripture. It once came very close. Dionysius of Corinth wrote about AD 170 that his church had read Rome's new letter on the Lord's day and would draw advice from it, "as also from the former epistle, which was written to us through Clement" (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11); Eusebius says it was read publicly "in a great many churches" (3.16); the fifth-century Codex Alexandrinus copies it after the books of the New Testament; and the Apostolic Canons name "two Epistles of Clemens" in their list of sacred books (canon 85). In one church family the question stayed open much longer: George Reid wrote in 1908 that "the Coptic-Arabic Church include with the canonical Scriptures the Apostolic Constitutions and the Clementine Epistles" (see "How the churches answer" below).
facts: Not in the New Testament of the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Ethiopian, Anglican, Reformed or Baptist churches (Trent; Reid, 1908; Cowley, 1974; Article VI; Westminster Confession). Reid (1908) wrote that the Coptic-Arabic Church included "the Clementine Epistles" with the canonical Scriptures, and Abū al-Barakāt Ibn Kabar (died 1324), in a work Villecourt called an encyclopedia of church learning "dans l'église copte", counted Clement's two letters in "the collection of books of the new law reckoned in the Church." Elsewhere it stood at the edge of the canon: read in church at Corinth and in many other churches (Eusebius, Church History 3.16; 4.23.11), copied after the New Testament in Codex Alexandrinus and named in that codex's table of New Testament books (Fenlon), named in the list of Apostolic Canon 85, and placed among the New Testament apocrypha in the Stichometry of Nicephorus (Westcott, Appendix D).

Unnamed in the letter, which speaks for the church of Rome (1:0). From the second century the tradition names Clement, a leader of the Roman church in the 90s (Dionysius of Corinth and Hegesippus in Eusebius; Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.3.3; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 15). Lake sees "no reason for rejecting this tradition."

Lake: after Nero's persecution (5) and after the apostles' time (42; 44), so not before about AD 75–80; while elders appointed by the apostles were still alive (44), so probably not much after 100. If the troubles of 1:1 are Domitian's, about AD 96, though "we know very little about the alleged persecution in the time of Domitian." His summary (1912): between 75 and 110, with "a general agreement among critics" for the last decade of the first century. Chapman wrote in 1908 that it was then "universally acknowledged, after Lightfoot" that the letter dates from about the last year of Domitian (Harnack) or just after his death in 96 (Funk); he names Grotius, Grabe, Orsi, Uhlhorn, Hefele and Wieseler as having dated it soon after Nero, and Volkmar and Baur as having placed it under Hadrian.

Rome, writing to Corinth after a few rash people (1:1) had stirred up a revolt and removed elders who had served without blame (44:3–6). The letter names Claudius Ephebus and Valerius Bito, "with Fortunatus too" (65:1); Lightfoot thought the wording may set Fortunatus apart as a Corinthian rather than a Roman messenger.

A letter of counsel to another church, built like a long sermon: lists of examples from Scripture and from recent history, long quotations of the Greek Old Testament, appeals to the order of nature, and a closing prayer (59–61).
Greek: "earnest and simple, restrained and dignified, and sometimes eloquent," and "correct, though not classical" (Chapman). Ancient translations into Latin, Syriac and Coptic survive.
65 chapters, 399 verses, plus the greeting, numbered 1:0 on this site.

The Greek printed by Kirsopp Lake (Loeb Classical Library, 1912), an eclectic text from Codex Alexandrinus (A, fifth century, which has lost a leaf from 57:7 to the end of chapter 63), the Codex Constantinopolitanus (C, AD 1056), the Latin, Syriac and Coptic versions, and the quotations of Clement of Alexandria (Lake; Lightfoot).
authorship: Nothing about its writer. It opens with the church of God in Rome greeting the church of God in Corinth (1:0), speaks throughout as "we," and names only the messengers (63:3; 65:1). In Lake's words, "it clearly claims to be not the letter of a single person but of a church."

About AD 170 Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, thanked the Romans for a new letter and said his church would read it "as also from the former epistle, which was written to us through Clement" (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11). Irenaeus, about 180, says that "in the time of this Clement" the church in Rome sent "a most powerful letter to the Corinthians" (Against Heresies 3.3.3). Eusebius calls it "acknowledged to be genuine" (3.16) and "accepted by all" (3.38.1), and Jerome says Clement "wrote, on the part of the church of Rome, an especially valuable Letter to the church of the Corinthians" (Lives of Illustrious Men 15). Lake: the tradition "is not supported by any corroborative evidence in its favour," but "there is nothing whatever against it." Both statements fit the letter itself: one man wrote it, in the name of his church.

Irenaeus makes him the third bishop of Rome "from the apostles," after Linus and Anacletus, and says he had seen the apostles (3.3.3). Jerome counts him fourth after Peter, adding that "most of the Latins" made him second (15). Chapman explains the different orders of the lists and notes that the Roman Canon of the Mass names "Linus, Cletus, Clemens." Lightfoot, an Anglican bishop and the great editor of Clement, judged the case that Clement was a bishop "as strong as the universal tradition of the next ages can make it," but held that he was "rather the chief of the presbyters than the chief over the presbyters" (The Christian Ministry, 63).

Paul greets Clement and the rest of his coworkers at Philippi (Philippians 4:3). Eusebius (3.4.10; 3.15) and Jerome (15) identify him with the Roman Clement, and Chapman adds Origen and Epiphanius, but judges that Paul's Clement "was probably a Philippian." Lake: "Tradition has naturally identified him" with that Clement. The name was common, and Philippians does not say.

In a vision in the Shepherd of Hermas, a Roman book of the second century, the woman who is the church tells Hermas to send one copy of his little book "to Clement," who "shall send it to the cities abroad, for that is his duty" (Vision 2.4.3, Lake's translation). Lake: this "certainly points to a Clement in Rome exercising the same functions as the writer of I. Clement," though Hermas is probably later and the line "may be merely a literary device."
Titus Flavius Clemens and the imperial household

Lake reports that Titus Flavius Clemens, a cousin of the emperor Domitian, "was in 95 A.D. accused of treason or impiety (ἀθεότης) by Domitian, his cousin, owing, according to Dio Cassius, to his Jewish proclivities," that he was put to death, and that his wife Domitilla was banished; and he adds, "There is no proof that he was really a Christian." Chapman calls the consul "martyred." Eusebius tells of a Flavia Domitilla, "daughter of a sister of Flavius Clement," exiled "in consequence of testimony borne to Christ" (Church History 3.18.5): a niece, where Lake, following Dio, has a wife. The sources opened for this page do not say whether these are two women or one. Lake thinks it "not probable" that the consul wrote the letter, but "an attractive and not improbable hypothesis" that a slave or freedman of the Flavian family bore the name Clemens and led the Roman church. Chapman agrees that "the ancients never suggest" the consul. Lightfoot notes that the messengers' names, Claudius and Valerius (65:1), "suggest some connexion with the imperial household," since the emperor Claudius belonged to the Claudian family and his empress Messalina to the Valerian, and judges it "fairly probable that they are in some way connected with the palace" (compare Philippians 4:22).

audience.to: The church at Corinth, the city in Greece to which Paul had written about forty years before, if the letter is from the 90s (47:1–3). A few of its members, "rash and headstrong" in the letter's words (1:1), had led a revolt and removed from office elders who had served without blame (44:3–6). The letter calls these men the leaders of the revolt (14:1; 51:1) and speaks to the whole church as "beloved." It was meant to be read aloud in the assembly and was carried by trusted men: "We have sent faithful and self-restrained men who have lived among us without blame from youth to old age. They will be witnesses between you and us." (63:3). It names Claudius Ephebus and Valerius Bito, "with Fortunatus too," who were to bring back news of peace (65:1). Lightfoot thought the wording may set Fortunatus apart, "perhaps not a Roman who accompanied the letter, but a Corinthian from whom Clement was expecting a visit," possibly the Fortunatus of 1 Corinthians 16:17, though "Fortunatus is a very common name." About AD 170 Dionysius of Corinth wrote that his church still drew advice from "the former epistle, which was written to us through Clement" (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11).
audience.why: To end the revolt and restore the elders. The letter tries to bring the Corinthians to repent, to humble themselves, and to return to peace and harmony (63:2; 65:1). It argues that God loves order, in the creation, in the army, in the body and in the Temple; that the apostles themselves set up the ministry and provided for its succession; and that removing faithful elders is a serious sin (44:4). It asks the ringleaders to leave rather than keep the church divided (54:1–2). Knowing the readers changes how the letter reads. Its long lists of jealousy and humility are not general moral lessons but aimed at a church split over its leaders, and its famous words on ministry (42–44) were written to defend particular men at Corinth, not to describe a whole system of church government.
views: Chapman (1908) wrote that it was then "universally acknowledged, after Lightfoot" to date from the last years of Domitian (died AD 96) or just after, reading the sudden misfortunes, one after another, that delayed it (1:1) as a persecution in Rome; he names Grotius, Grabe, Orsi, Uhlhorn, Hefele and Wieseler for a date soon after Nero. Lake (1912) reports "a general agreement among critics" for the last decade of the first century, but keeps the date open between 75 and 110 because "we know very little about the alleged persecution in the time of Domitian."
Did Corinth ask Rome for help?

The letter says it is late in turning to the matters in dispute at Corinth (1:1). Chapman thinks "no appeal seems to have been made to Rome": the Roman church wrote on its own to restore peace. How far the letter shows an authority of the Roman church, or of its bishop, over another church is argued (see the section "Rome, Corinth and authority").

The letter does not say why the elders were removed, only that they were blameless and that a few rash people led the revolt, "one or two persons" as Lake's English has it in another place (1:1; 44:6; 47:6). Lightfoot read it as "a spirit of insubordination" in which faithful presbyters were "ruthlessly expelled from office" (The Christian Ministry, 38). We hear only Rome's side.

outline: The greeting; Corinth's famous good name; how prosperity led to jealousy and revolt
What jealousy and envy have done: Cain and Abel to David and Saul, then Peter, Paul and the martyrs of Clement's own day
Repent and obey: Noah and Jonah, Enoch, Abraham, Lot and Rahab, saved by faith and hospitality
Be humble: the words of the Lord Jesus, Christ the humble servant of Isaiah 53 and Psalm 22, the prophets, Abraham, Job, Moses and David's Psalm 51
The harmony of the creation: sky, earth, sea and seasons keep the order God gave them
Live worthily: the household and the church; Psalm 34; the double-minded
The resurrection: day and night, the seed, the phoenix, the promises of the Psalms and Job
God sees everything: draw near to him as his chosen portion; leave pride behind
The way of blessing: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; made right not through ourselves but through faith; still eager for good works; God's gifts; Jesus Christ the high priest
Order in the army and the body; let no one boast; Job against the proud
The order of worship in the Temple: high priest, priests, Levites and the layperson
The apostles appointed overseers and deacons and provided for successors; Moses and Aaron's rod; removing blameless men is a sin
The righteous suffer but are not thrown out by the holy; Daniel and the three young men; why is there strife? Take up Paul's letter to you

Confess and repent; Moses who offered himself for the people; let the leaders of the revolt leave; kings, Christians, Judith and Esther who gave themselves for others; submit to the elders; Wisdom's warning from Proverbs 1
The great prayer: for the chosen, the afflicted and the rulers
Summary; the messengers sent from Rome; the blessing

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Reads the letter as a document of the Roman church at the end of the first century: its date (Lake's 75–110 and the case for the 90s), its writer, what happened at Corinth, the manuscripts and versions, and the sources it draws on (Hebrews, 1 Corinthians, Jewish lists of examples, Greek and Roman commonplaces).

lenses.name: New Testament
lenses.desc: Sets the letter beside the New Testament it knows and the generation that wrote it: 1 Corinthians (47), Hebrews (17:1; 36), Paul and James on faith and works (30–33), Peter and Paul (5), the sayings of Jesus it quotes in forms of its own (13:2; 46:8), and the Pastoral Letters and Acts on overseers and elders (42–44).

lenses.name: Jewish Scripture and the Septuagint
lenses.desc: How a Roman Christian reads Israel's Scriptures in Greek: long quotations of the Septuagint (Isaiah 53 and Psalm 51 whole), the Greek Isaiah 60:17 behind "overseers and deacons," Jewish lists of examples, Judith and Esther, the Temple service as a pattern (40–41), and the shape of Jewish prayer behind 59–61.

lenses.name: Church order and the churches
lenses.desc: What 40–44 says about the ministry and how the churches read it: succession from the apostles, overseers (bishops) and elders, whether a congregation may remove its ministers, and the place of the Roman church. A Catholic and an Anglican reading from writers who address the letter itself (Chapman, Lightfoot), with the site's cards for the wider questions.

lenses.name: Greek and Roman world
lenses.desc: The letter in its city and empire: the political language of concord and civil strife (homonoia, stasis), the Roman army (37), the old fable of the body (37–38), the ordered cosmos (20), the phoenix (25), and the women martyrs called Danaids and Dirces (6:2).

sections.b:
The Plain English Translation is made for this site from the Greek printed by Kirsopp Lake in the Loeb Apostolic Fathers (vol. 1, 1912), as digitized by First1KGreek and corrected against the scans of Lake's page. Lake's text is eclectic: of the witnesses, he writes, "none of them can be regarded as undoubtedly superior to the others, so that any critical text is necessarily eclectic," though "there is very little range of variation." Every place where the Plain English Translation leaves Lake's text, and every reading in his notes that changes the meaning, has a variant entry.

The greeting is numbered 1:0, as the site numbers the titles of the Psalms. The English check text offered beside the Greek is Lake's own translation (public domain). The letter quotes the Greek Old Testament, often at length: where its Greek matches the verse the site has translated from the Hebrew, the Plain English Translation uses the site's wording; where the Septuagint or the writer differs, it translates what the letter says, and a note shows the difference.

sections.h: The Roman church and the Corinthian revolt
sections.b:
The occasion is plain from the letter itself. At Corinth, a few rash and headstrong people (1:1) had stirred up a revolt (Greek stasis, the word for faction and civil strife in a Greek city) and removed elders who had served the flock of Christ without blame (44:3). The letter calls this the worst news about Corinth since Paul's day, worse than the factions of Paul, Cephas and Apollos (47:3–4), because then they had taken sides with apostles and with a man the apostles approved, while now the old church of Corinth is rebelling against its elders because of one or two people (47:4–6).

Rome does not order; it pleads, argues and prays. It reminds the Corinthians of their old good name (1–2), shows them what jealousy has always done (3–6), and fills more than half the letter with examples of repentance, faith, humility, order and love before it reaches the ministry (40–44). Its answer is that those who caused the trouble should repent and, if need be, leave (54), and that the removed elders should be restored. Lake sums up its aim as a protest "against this deposition, and the partizanship which has caused it." The letter ends with a long prayer (59–61; see "The great prayer").

Lake's argument runs from the letter itself. Chapter 5 looks back on the deaths of Peter and Paul, so it is later than Nero's persecution; chapters 42 and 44 treat the apostles' time as past; so "it can therefore scarcely be older than 75–80 A.D." On the other hand, chapter 44 speaks of elders appointed by the apostles who are still alive, and there is "no trace of any of the controversies or persecutions of the second century," so it is "probably not much later than 100 A.D." If the sudden misfortunes of 1:1 are a persecution under Domitian, the letter dates from about 96. Lake is careful: "we know very little about the alleged persecution in the time of Domitian," and it would not be prudent to rule out a date ten or fifteen years later. His conclusion: between 75 and 110, with "a general agreement among critics" for the last decade of the first century.

The early witnesses fit that range. Hegesippus, in the mid-second century, is "a trustworthy witness" that a sedition happened at Corinth in Clement's time (Eusebius, Church History 3.16), and Irenaeus places the letter in the time of Clement, the third bishop after the apostles (Against Heresies 3.3.3).

Other dates have had their holders. Chapman, writing in 1908, found it "strange that even a few good scholars (such as Grotius Grabe, Orsi, Uhlhorn, Hefele, Wieseler) should have dated it soon after Nero." He reports that Volkmar placed it under Hadrian, because he dated the Book of Judith, which the letter uses (55), to that reign, and that Baur followed him "but not" Hilgenfeld; Chapman answers that the letter of Polycarp already borrows from Clement. His own verdict, "now universally acknowledged, after Lightfoot," was the last year of Domitian (Harnack) or just after his death in 96 (Funk). That was the state of the question in 1908; the sources opened for this page give no later survey of scholarly opinion.

Chapter 5 holds an account from the generation after the apostles of how Peter and Paul ended their lives. It is short, and it is worth reading for what it does and does not say: "There was Peter. He suffered under unrighteous jealousy, and his hardships were not one or two but many. Having borne his witness so, he went on to the place of glory owed to him." Then: "Because of jealousy and fighting Paul showed the way to the prize that endurance wins. Seven times he wore chains. He was banished, he was stoned. He became a herald in the East and in the West, and he won the noble fame of his faith. He taught righteousness to the whole world and came to the far limit of the West. And having borne his witness before the rulers, he was set free from the world in this way and taken up into the holy place, the greatest model of endurance for others to trace." (5:4–7). A great multitude of the chosen joined them in suffering, among them women who suffered "as Danaids and Dirces," figures of Greek myth (6:1–2).

The Greek verb for "borne his witness" (martyrēsas) is the verb behind "martyr"; whether it already means "died as a martyr" here, or "testified," is a question the notes at 5:4 and 5:7 take up. The chapter does not name Rome, Nero or the way either apostle died. Chapman (1908) judged that "these two Apostles are mentioned because they suffered at Rome," and that "it seems that St. Paul went to Spain as he intended (Romans 15:28)"; "the far limit of the West" (to terma tēs dyseōs) has been read both as Spain and in other ways, and the note at 5:7 sets out who holds each reading. Several notes elsewhere on the site lean on this chapter for Paul's death "in Rome under Nero": that comes from later writers such as Eusebius (Church History 2.25), not from Clement's words.

sections.h: The ministry of chapters 40–44, and how the churches read it
sections.b:
The best-known pages of the letter argue from order. God gave the Temple its proper times and places and its ranks: the high priest, the priests, the Levites, and the layperson, bound by the rules for laypeople (40:5; Greek laikos, one of the people). In the same way, Christ was sent from God and the apostles from Christ; they preached in country and town and appointed their firstfruits, tested by the Spirit, as overseers and deacons, as the Greek Isaiah 60:17 had foretold (42:1–5). Then the sentence on which the debate turns: "Through our Lord Jesus Christ, our apostles also knew that the title of overseer would be fought over. That is why, since they had been given full knowledge ahead of time, they appointed the men already named. Afterward they added a rule that if they fell asleep, other tested men should take over their service." (44:1–2). So it is not right to remove men appointed by the apostles, or later by other respected men with the whole church agreeing, who have served blamelessly (44:3).

The churches read this passage with different emphases. Each view below is given from a writer who addresses 1 Clement itself; the site's cards on the wider questions are at Acts 1 and 2 Timothy 2 (succession from the apostles), Acts 14 (who chooses elders), and 1 Timothy 3, Acts 20, Philippians 1 and Titus 1 (bishops and elders).

  • A Catholic reading. Chapman, writing in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1908), takes the passage to show "that the Apostles provided for a lawful succession of ministers," and notes that the overseers and deacons of 44 "cannot be removed at pleasure." He also grants that in the letter "presbyters are mentioned several times, but are not distinguished from bishops," and that "there is absolutely no mention of a bishop at Corinth."
  • An Anglican reading. Lightfoot, bishop of Durham, read the passage as providing "for a succession in the ministry" by elders appointed by the apostles or by those they appointed, but found "no mention of episcopacy, properly so called, throughout the epistle; for in the language of St Clement, 'bishop' and 'presbyter' are still synonymous terms" (The Christian Ministry, 38). He therefore took the "they" of 44:2 to mean the first elders, not the apostles.
  • Who are "they" in 44:2? Some readers, among them Rothe and Michiels as Chapman reports, take the clause to mean "if they, the Apostles, should fall asleep," so that the apostles provided successors to themselves; Chapman calls this reading awkward, and Lightfoot rejects it. The word for the rule is uncertain in the manuscripts (epinomē in A, epidomē in C, the Latin legem), and Lightfoot proposed epimonē, "permanence" (Lake's note): see the variant at 44:2.

On the Orthodox, Reformed, Baptist and other free-church readings, this page cites nothing that addresses 1 Clement directly; their views on bishops, elders and succession are given on the site's cards named above.

Here is a church writing at length to another church, and later warning: "But if some disobey what God has said through us, let them know that they will tie themselves up in wrongdoing and in no small danger." (59:1). Catholic readers have seen in this an early exercise of the Roman church's authority. Chapman, in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1908): Clement "evidently writes officially, with all that authority of the Roman Church of which Ignatius and Irenaeus have so much to say." Chapman also quotes the Anglican Lightfoot on the letter's tone of authority: "It may, perhaps, seem strange ... to describe this noble remonstrance as the first step towards papal domination. And yet undoubtedly this is the case" (Lightfoot, vol. 1, p. 70, as Chapman quotes him). Chapman reports the other side of Lightfoot and of Harnack too: they liked to point out "that we hear earlier of the importance of the Roman Church than of the authority of the Roman bishop," since the letter speaks for a church, not for one man, and it argues and pleads rather than commands. Lightfoot added that if Clement was bishop he was "rather the chief of the presbyters than the chief over the presbyters" (The Christian Ministry, 63). This page cites no Orthodox or Protestant writer on 59:1 itself. The site's cards on Peter and his successors are at Matthew 16 and Luke 22.

Near the end the letter turns into a long prayer, asking God, the Creator of the universe, to keep the number of his chosen, to save the afflicted, raise the fallen, feed the hungry and free the prisoners, and to give peace and harmony to all who live on the earth (59–60). Then it prays for the rulers, the same Roman authorities under whom Christians had just suffered: God gave them their power, so Christians submit to them, and the church asks God to give them health, peace, harmony and stability so that they may govern without stumbling (61:1–2). It ends with praise through Jesus Christ, the high priest and guardian of our souls (61:3).

Chapman calls it "a beautiful Eucharistic prayer" and notes that Lightfoot discussed the "liturgical character" of parts of the letter at length; Duchesne, as Chapman quotes him, would not call it "a reproduction of a sacred formulary" but "an excellent example of the style of solemn prayer" used at the church's meetings for worship. The prayer for rulers stands beside Romans 13:1–7, 1 Timothy 2:1–2, Titus 3:1 and 1 Peter 2:13–17. Codex Alexandrinus is missing a page here, so most of the prayer rests on the Codex Constantinopolitanus and the versions (see the next section).

sections.h: Codex Alexandrinus, the versions and Clement of Alexandria
sections.b:
Codex Alexandrinus (A), a Greek Bible of the fifth century (in the British Museum when Lake wrote), copies the Old and New Testaments and after them the two letters that go under Clement's name. It has lost a leaf of 1 Clement, from 57:7 to the end of chapter 63, and the end of 2 Clement (Lake's note at 57:6; Lightfoot; Fenlon in the Catholic Encyclopedia). The letters were first printed from it by Patrick Young in 1633 (Chapman). In 1875 Bryennios published the whole text from the Codex Constantinopolitanus (C), written by Leo the Notary in 1056, which also contains 2 Clement, the Epistle of Barnabas, the Didache and the long form of the Letters of Ignatius (Lake). Lake lists four more witnesses: a Syriac version in one manuscript of 1169 at Cambridge (University Library Add. 1700), "probably not early"; a Latin version in one manuscript of the eleventh century from Florennes, now at Namur, but "extremely ancient," which "may perhaps be best regarded" as made in Rome in the late second or early third century; a Coptic version in two manuscripts, a fourth-century papyrus in Berlin and a later, broken manuscript in Strassburg; and the quotations in the Stromata of Clement of Alexandria (about AD 200). In the Syriac manuscript, Lightfoot notes, the letters of Clement are "incorporated among the Epistles of the New Testament in the Philoxenian (Harclean) version."

So for 57:7–63:4 the Greek rests on C alone, checked against the Syriac, Latin and Coptic; the chapter pages and variants there say so.

sections.h: The letter at the edge of the canon
sections.b:
Few writings outside the New Testament came so close to it. The evidence, in order:

  • Read in church. About AD 170 Dionysius of Corinth wrote to Rome: "Today we have passed the Lord's holy day, in which we have read your epistle. From it, whenever we read it, we shall always be able to draw advice, as also from the former epistle, which was written to us through Clement" (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11). Eusebius took this to show "that it had been the custom from the beginning to read it in the church"; he says the letter "has been publicly used in a great many churches both in former times and in our own" (3.16), and Jerome that it "in some places is publicly read" (Lives of Illustrious Men 15).
  • Quoted with honor. Clement of Alexandria calls its writer "the Apostle Clement" (Stromata 4.17), and Lake judges that he "appears" to treat it as Scripture. Eusebius says Clement of Alexandria used testimonies from "the disputed Scriptures," among them those of Barnabas "and Clement" (6.13.6).
  • Copied with the Bible. In Codex Alexandrinus it follows the New Testament, and the codex's own table of contents names the two letters of Clement among the New Testament books; Fenlon, in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1908), concludes that they "seem to have been regarded by the scribe as part of the New Testament." Swete adds that the same table puts the Psalms of Solomon "after the final summary of the books of the Old and New Testaments," with 2 Clement as "the book which in the list immediately precedes them." In the Strassburg Coptic manuscript, Lake says, it is "directly joined on to the canonical books," and from both he suggests that "at an early period in Alexandria and Egypt I. Clement was regarded as part of the New Testament." Westcott, judging by the standard of "our own Church," saw it differently: placed after the Apocalypse, it held "a position similar to that of the Apocryphal books of the Old Testament, according to the judgment of our own Church" (522).
  • Named in one list, set apart in others. The Apostolic Canons, in the last canon, give a list of books to be "counted venerable and sacred." After "Our own books, that is, those of the New Testament," the Gospels and the letters of Paul, Peter, John, James and Jude, it adds "Two Epistles of Clemens, and the Constitutions of me Clemens," and ends with "the Acts of us the Apostles"; it has no Revelation (canon 85). Westcott (1896) calls this catalogue "curious; but as a piece of evidence it is of no value. It was drawn, I believe, from Syrian sources, and probably dates from the sixth century" (446), and says "the peculiarities of this Catalogue received no conciliar sanction" (522). The Council in Trullo (692) confirmed the eighty-five canons but rejected the Constitutions because heretics had brought in "adulterous matter" (canon 2), and said nothing of the letters. The Stichometry attached to the Chronography of Nicephorus (patriarch 806–814) lists "Clement 1, 2" with the Teaching of the Apostles among the apocrypha of the New Testament (Westcott, Appendix D). Eusebius, though he calls the letter genuine and accepted by all, does not name it in his list of the accepted, disputed and rejected books (3.25), and Athanasius names it neither among the books of the New Testament nor among the books, "not indeed included in the Canon," that new believers may read: the Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit, the Teaching of the Apostles and the Shepherd (Festal Letter 39).

The letter knows several New Testament writings and quotes the sayings of Jesus. It names one: it tells the Corinthians to take up the letter of the blessed apostle Paul (47:1), his first letter to Corinth, which already rebuked the Corinthians for taking sides with Paul, Cephas and Apollos (47:3; 1 Corinthians 1:12). Its praise of love (49) runs close to 1 Corinthians 13:4–7, and its body of many members (37:5–38:1) to 1 Corinthians 12:12–27. Its picture of Jesus Christ as high priest, as much greater than the angels as his name is more excellent (36:2), uses the chain of quotations that opens Hebrews (Hebrews 1:3–13); Eusebius already noticed that Clement "gives many thoughts drawn from the Epistle to the Hebrews, and also quotes verbally some of its expressions" (Church History 3.38.1), and reported that "some say that the evangelist Luke, others that this Clement himself, translated the epistle" into Greek (3.38.2–3). Jerome thought the two letters alike in style, though different in ideas and word order (15). Twice the letter quotes words of "the Lord Jesus" in forms close to, but not the same as, the Gospels (13:2; 46:8): the notes there set them side by side.

On faith and works, Clement says both that we are made right not through ourselves but through faith (32:4) and that we must not be lazy in doing good (33:1), and he praises Abraham and Rahab for faith and hospitality (10; 12) in the manner of James 2:21–25. The chapter pages for 31–33 give the readings.

spec.title: Claude's theory: Clement borrows Paul's own word for order
spec.body: In 1 Corinthians 15:23 Paul says that in the resurrection each one comes in his own order (Greek en tō idiō tagmati), using a military word for a unit or rank. 1 Clement, which tells the Corinthians to "take up" that very letter (47:1), uses the same phrase twice in its argument for order: of soldiers who each carry out the emperor's commands in his own rank (37:3), and of each Christian, who should please God in his own rank (41:1). The site's note at 1 Corinthians 15:23 already cites 1 Clement 37 for the same army picture, so the shared picture is not new. My suggestion goes one step further: the repeated phrase may be a deliberate echo, aimed at readers who knew Paul's letter, so that Paul's word for the order of the resurrection becomes Clement's word for order in the church. Lake and Lightfoot, in the pages opened for this book, do not make that link, and it rests only on the shared phrase.

spec.title: Claude's theory: seven old examples and a seven-times-chained apostle
spec.body: Chapter 4 gives exactly seven examples of jealousy from Israel's Scriptures: Cain and Abel (4:1–7), Jacob and Esau (4:8), Joseph (4:9), Moses (4:10), Aaron and Miriam (4:11), Dathan and Abiram (4:12) and David under Saul (4:13). Chapter 5 then turns to the examples of Clement's own generation, and the first detail it gives about Paul is that he wore chains seven times (5:6). Seven is a number of completeness in Scripture (see the topic Numbers in the Bible). The list may be built to that number, with Paul's sevenfold chains as a quiet answer: a complete record of what jealousy did, then a complete endurance under it. The count could also be accident. The commentators opened for this page (Lake, Lightfoot, Chapman) note the list and the seven imprisonments but do not connect the two numbers; the connection is mine.

prompts: Two elderly men in plain cloaks, one carrying a rolled letter tied with cord, stand on a stone harbor quay at Ostia with a merchant ship behind them, its square sail half raised; behind them on a hill a small group of Christians in tunics raise their hands in prayer; in the far distance the outline of Rome's walls. Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll, sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like cave paintings, small Greek letters along the margin, a few bold flat shapes of deep blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs; soft, torn edges fading into the parchment, never a hard rectangle.

A circular diagram drawn like an old map of the world: the sun and moon and a ring of stars turning in their courses above, the four seasons as small figures handing a torch from one to the next, the sea held back by a line of shore, rivers running down from hills, and at the edges a faint ocean with unknown lands beyond it; a Greek word for harmony written along the top. Style: hand-sketched onto a parchment scroll in sepia ink and soft watercolor washes of ochre and blue, with cave-painting animals grazing in the fields and a modern-art flatness to the sky; soft edges, no frame.

A great bird with red and gold feathers rising from a small nest of spices and myrrh, a small worm in the ashes below beginning to grow wings, and behind it the obelisks and temple of the Sun at Heliopolis in Egypt under a low sun; a robed priest with a tablet counts the years. Style: sketched onto an ancient scroll in ink and charcoal with Egyptian hieroglyphic register lines and red-ochre pigment, mixed with a few bold flat modern shapes; soft, faded edges blending into the parchment.

canon.summary: 1 Clement is a letter of the church of Rome to the church of Corinth from the end of the first century, by tradition written by Clement of Rome. It is not in the New Testament of the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Ethiopian, Anglican, Reformed or Baptist churches. In the early church it came close to the canon: it was read in church at Corinth and elsewhere, copied after the New Testament in Codex Alexandrinus, and named in the list of the Apostolic Canons, but the main lists left it out. Reid (1908) reports that the Coptic-Arabic Church counted "the Clementine Epistles" with its canonical Scriptures, and the Arabic catalogue of Abū al-Barakāt (died 1324) counts Clement's two letters among "the books of the new law reckoned in the Church."
accepted_by: Not Scripture: the Council of Trent's list of the New Testament books (1546) does not include it. John Chapman, in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1908), wrote that "His feast is celebrated 23 November," noted that the Roman Canon of the Mass names "Linus, Cletus, Clemens," and called the letter Clement's one "genuine writing."

Not in the New Testament as Reid (1908) describes it: the Eastern Orthodox churches "have a New Testament identical with the Catholic." The older canons leave a tension. The Apostolic Canons name "Two Epistles of Clemens" right after "our own books, that is, those of the New Testament" (canon 85), and the Council in Trullo (692) confirmed the eighty-five canons, rejecting only the Constitutions named beside the letters (canon 2). Westcott (1896) points out that at Trullo "no notice was taken of the two Clementine epistles which were also pronounced Canonical at the same time" (446); he judges that "the peculiarities of this Catalogue received no conciliar sanction" (522), and that the later history of the Greek Church shows that Trullo's ratification of the earlier councils' canons "was not supposed to fix definitely (which indeed it could not do) the contents of Holy Scripture" (446). This page found no present-day Orthodox statement that names 1 Clement in or out of the New Testament. The Orthodox Church in America commemorates "the Hieromartyr Clement, Pope of Rome" on November 25 and says he left "two Epistles to the Corinthians," "the first written examples of Christian teaching after the writings of the holy Apostles."

Not in its Bible. The church's list of its 35 New Testament books includes "The book of Clement" (no. 34), listed after the Sirate Tsion ("the book of order") and before the Didascalia. R. W. Cowley (1974) describes that book as "a book in seven parts, communicated by Peter to Clement," and says "it is not the Roman or Corinthian correspondence."

Here the sources say the letters were counted with the New Testament. Abū al-Barakāt Ibn Kabar (died 1324), a presbyter whose encyclopedia of church learning Villecourt placed "dans l'église copte", says that Clement "has two letters, which the 318 appointed. They make up one book from the collection of books of the new law reckoned in the Church" (trans. McCollum). George Reid wrote in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1908) that "the Coptic-Arabic Church include with the canonical Scriptures the Apostolic Constitutions and the Clementine Epistles." The letter was translated into Coptic early: Lake describes a fourth-century papyrus in Berlin and a later manuscript in Strassburg in which it is "directly joined on to the canonical books." This page found no present-day statement of the Coptic Orthodox Church on the matter, so it cannot say whether Coptic Bibles print the letter today.

In the one Syriac manuscript of the letter (Cambridge University Library Add. 1700, of 1169 in Lake's dating), Lightfoot found the letters of Clement "incorporated among the Epistles of the New Testament in the Philoxenian (Harclean) version"; Lake thinks this Syriac version "probably not early." Reid's survey (1908) mentions no letters of Clement in the Armenian New Testament. This page found no statement of the Syriac Orthodox or Armenian churches that names 1 Clement.

Not Scripture. Article VI receives "all the Books of the New Testament, as they are commonly received"; 1 Clement is not one of them, nor among the "other Books" the Church reads for example of life. The Anglican bishop J. B. Lightfoot made the standard edition and commentary.

Westcott (1896) wrote that "the Lutheran Church has no recognised definition of Canonicity, and no express list of the Sacred Books," and that usage settled the place of the disputed books. This page found no Lutheran statement that names 1 Clement.

Not Scripture. The Westminster Confession lists the 27 books of the New Testament, "given by inspiration of God, to be the rule of faith and life" (1.2), and says that "the books commonly called Apocrypha" are "no part of the canon of Scripture" (1.3). It does not mention early Christian writings such as 1 Clement; the letter is simply not in its list.

Not Scripture. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689) lists the same 27 New Testament books (1.2) and, like Westminster, rejects "the books commonly called Apocrypha" (1.3). It does not mention 1 Clement, which is not in its list.

provenance.h: From Rome to Corinth, probably in the 90s
provenance.b: The letter was written in Greek by a leader of the Roman church, on behalf of the whole church, and sent to Corinth by messengers named in 65:1, after some members there removed their elders (44:6). Its date, by Lake's reasoning from the letter itself, lies between 75 and 110, with "a general agreement among critics" for the 90s (see "When was it written?").

About 170 Dionysius of Corinth wrote that his church would keep drawing advice from "the former epistle, which was written to us through Clement," and Eusebius took his words to show that "it had been the custom from the beginning to read it in the church" (Church History 4.23.11). Hegesippus knew of it in the mid-second century (Eusebius 3.16; 4.22.1), Irenaeus describes it about 180 (Against Heresies 3.3.3), and Clement of Alexandria quotes it often (Lake). Lake thinks the Latin version "may perhaps be best regarded as a translation of the late second or early third century made in Rome"; a Coptic version survives in a fourth-century papyrus, and the Syriac is later (Lake). It was copied with the books of the Bible in Codex Alexandrinus, whose letters and history, Fenlon judged in 1908, "point to Egypt as its place of origin," and in the Strassburg Coptic manuscript.

Its one Latin manuscript, of the eleventh century, comes from the monastery of Florennes (Lake). The first printed edition was made from Codex Alexandrinus by Patrick Young in 1633 (Chapman). The full Greek text appeared only in 1875, from the Constantinople manuscript; the Syriac was published in full in 1899, the Latin in 1894 and the Coptic in 1908 and 1910 (Lake).

• The Greek Old Testament, quoted at great length: Isaiah 53 (16), Psalm 51 (18), Psalm 34 (22), Proverbs 1 (57), with examples from Genesis to Daniel (4; 9–12; 17; 45; 51–55).
  • Paul's letters, above all 1 Corinthians, which it names (47:1), and probably Romans (32–35).
  • Hebrews, on Christ the high priest and the heroes of faith (36; 17:1), as Eusebius already saw (3.38.1).
  • The sayings of Jesus (13:2; 46:8).
  • Judith and Esther (55:4–6).

rejected_why.b: 1 Clement does not claim an apostle as its writer; it speaks for the church of Rome, looks back on the apostles as men of the past generation (5; 42; 44), and names no writer at all. Even those who honored it most, like Eusebius, called it the genuine letter "of this Clement" (3.16), a bishop after the apostles, not an apostolic book. Westcott argued that the high honor paid to the writings of Clement, Barnabas and Hermas, which still did not make them canonical, "becomes an indirect evidence of the implicit reverence paid to the Apostolic words, and of the Apostolic basis of the Canon" (522).

rejected_why.h: Honored, read, but left off the lists
rejected_why.b: Eusebius calls the letter genuine and widely read, yet in his catalogue of the New Testament writings, accepted, disputed and rejected, he does not name it at all (3.25). Athanasius's list of the New Testament (367) leaves it out, and so does his list of the books outside the canon that new believers may read: the Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit, the Teaching of the Apostles and the Shepherd (Festal Letter 39). The Stichometry of Nicephorus places it among the New Testament apocrypha (Westcott, Appendix D). The Apostolic Canons name it after the New Testament books, together with the Apostolic Constitutions under Clement's name, a work that the Council in Trullo (692) rejected (canon 2); Westcott calls that catalogue "of no value" as evidence and probably of the sixth century (446), and writes that "no one of these writings is reckoned among the Canonical books in any Catalogue of the Scriptures," with that list as the only apparent exception (522).

rejected_why.h: Kept at the end of the Bible
rejected_why.b: Where it was copied with the Bible, it stood after the New Testament. How the copyists counted it is read in two ways. Westcott saw in its place after the Apocalypse in Codex Alexandrinus "a position similar to that of the Apocryphal books of the Old Testament, according to the judgment of our own Church" (522). Fenlon, in the Catholic Encyclopedia, points out that the codex's own table of contents includes the letters in its list of New Testament books, so that they "seem to have been regarded by the scribe as part of the New Testament," and Lake says the same of Egypt "at an early period." Jerome's word that it "in some places is publicly read" (15) describes a local custom, not the practice of the whole church.

cited_in.b: Paul greets a Clement among his coworkers at Philippi. Eusebius (3.4.10; 3.15) and Jerome (15) identify him with the Roman Clement to whom the letter is credited; Chapman thinks Paul's Clement "was probably a Philippian," and the name was common. Even if the identification is right, Philippians says nothing of the letter.

1 Clement 36:2–5 draws on the opening chain of Hebrews: greater than the angels, angels made winds, "You are my son," "Sit at my right hand." Eusebius saw that Clement drew "many thoughts" from Hebrews and quoted some of its words (Church History 3.38.1), and reported that "some say that the evangelist Luke, others that this Clement himself, translated the epistle" (3.38.2), the second of which he thought "more probable" on grounds of style (3.38.3). The direction is that 1 Clement uses Hebrews; for who has been proposed as Hebrews' author, see the authorship table on the Hebrews page.

1 Clement tells the Corinthians to take up Paul's letter to them, written when they had taken sides with Paul, Cephas and Apollos (47:1–3). It names a letter of Paul and shows the Corinthian church still keeping and reading that letter a generation later.
The praise of love in 49:4–50:1 follows Paul's hymn in thought and in some words (love bears all things, is patient, is not arrogant); it is an echo of Paul, not a source for him.

Like James, 1 Clement holds up Abraham and Rahab together. Clement says that Abraham was given a son, and Rahab was saved, because of faith and hospitality (10:7; 12:1). Whether Clement knew James or both drew on a common Jewish way of telling these stories is not settled; the chapter pages give the readings.

The prayer for rulers in 60:4–61:2 does what 1 Timothy 2:1–2 asks, praying for kings and all in authority so that Christians may live in peace. It also shares the teaching of Romans 13:1 that their authority comes from God.

Acts 20 calls the elders of Ephesus overseers who shepherd the flock; 1 Clement likewise uses overseer and elder for the same men (42:4; 44:4–5) and speaks of the flock of Christ (44:3). Lightfoot drew from this that "bishop" and "presbyter" were still "synonymous terms" (The Christian Ministry, 38).

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to what a leading church believed and practiced at the end of the first century, 1 Clement is of the first rank: it is early, its place and approximate date are fairly secure, and it shows in its own words how Roman Christians read the Greek Old Testament, honored Peter and Paul, prayed, and thought about ministry. Its text is well preserved for so old a writing, with two Greek manuscripts and three ancient translations, though one leaf of the oldest Greek manuscript is lost. Its historical statements are few and brief, and where it speaks of recent events (the deaths of the apostles, the Corinthian revolt) it is a valuable but one-sided witness. Measured against the 66 books it agrees closely with them and goes beyond them mainly on church order, where Christians read it differently.

sections.h: 1. A witness to the church after the apostles: very high
sections.b: The letter comes from Rome within a generation of Peter and Paul, and it was read as Clement's work from the second century on (Dionysius, Hegesippus and Irenaeus, in Eusebius and Irenaeus). It shows a church that read the Greek Old Testament as its own Scripture, quoted Paul and Hebrews, prayed for the emperors under whom it had suffered, and cared about order and peace in other churches.

Two Greek manuscripts survive, of the fifth century (A) and of 1056 (C), with a Latin version that Lake judges "extremely ancient," a Syriac version, a Coptic version in a fourth-century papyrus, and many quotations in Clement of Alexandria. Lake finds "very little range of variation" and few readings in serious doubt. The weak point is 57:7–63:4, where A has lost a page and the Greek rests on C alone with the versions. A few readings change the sense, above all the word at 44:2 on which the succession sentence turns.

The letter says little about events, and it does not claim to be by an apostle, so it raises no problem of a false author. Its few historical statements are valuable: Peter's many sufferings and witness, Paul's seven imprisonments and his journey to the limit of the west (5), a great multitude of Christian martyrs, among them women (6), and the removal of elders at Corinth (44). But it gives no place, emperor or manner of death for the apostles, and later details (Rome, Nero, crucifixion, beheading) come from later writers. On the Corinthian revolt we have only Rome's side.

• Matches: God the Creator and Master of all; Jesus Christ the Lord, through whom God chose us (59:3; 64:1); his blood shed for our salvation (7:4; 12:7); the resurrection, with Christ as its firstfruits (24:1, as 1 Corinthians 15:20); being made right through faith and not through ourselves (32:4, as Romans 3:28), joined to eagerness for good works (33:1, as Ephesians 2:10 and Titus 2:14); love (49–50, as 1 Corinthians 13); prayer for rulers (61, as 1 Timothy 2:1–2).
  • Goes beyond: it uses the Temple's ranks of high priest, priests, Levites and layperson as a pattern for the church's order (40–41), and it says the apostles "added a rule" for the succession of those they appointed (44:2). That rule says more about how the ministry was to continue than the New Testament does, but both the word for "rule" and the meaning of "they" are uncertain (see the variant and notes at 44:2), so how far it goes beyond depends on the reading. How the churches read 40–44 is set out in the section on those chapters (Chapman for a Catholic reading, Lightfoot for an Anglican one) and in the cards at Acts 1, Acts 14 and 2 Timothy 2. It also uses the phoenix as a sign of the resurrection (25), a story from Greek writers, not from Scripture.
  • Tension, not conflict: Chapman writes that Clement "speaks strongly of justification by works," while 32:4 states justification through faith in Paul's own terms. The chapter pages for 31–33 give the readings and point to the Romans 3 and James 2 cards. In Claude's analysis the letter nowhere plainly conflicts with the 66 books.

how_to_read.b: 1 Clement is not in the Bible of the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Ethiopian, Anglican, Reformed or Baptist churches; if you belong to the Coptic church, see what this page reports under "How the churches answer." Read it as a letter from the church of the generation after the apostles: a window into how they prayed, read Scripture and settled a quarrel, not a word of God addressed to you with the authority of the apostles.

It was written to one church in one crisis. Its long examples and its words on ministry (42–44) aim at a particular revolt in Corinth. Ask first what it meant to them before using it to settle later questions about bishops or the papacy.

how_to_read.h: Read it with its Bible open
how_to_read.b: About a quarter of the letter quotes the Greek Old Testament. Look up its quotations, and notice where its Greek Bible differs from the Hebrew behind most English Old Testaments: the notes mark each difference.
Chapters 59–61 are an early Christian prayer, prayed by a church that had suffered for its rulers as well as for itself. They can be read and prayed today by Christians of any tradition.
